newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Leaders say arms talks vital to Europe stability.
newsitem.headline: Leaders say arms talks vital to Europe stability.

text.p: A European security summit agreed on Monday to new talks to update a Cold War-era pact on arms reductions, a move hailed by leaders as a crucial step towards maintaining lasting stability in an undivided Europe.
The agreement on a fresh round of talks to adapt the 1990 arms cuts treaty was announced at the start of a two-day summit of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
"This is a major achievement which, by itself, will justify this summit," Portuguese Prime Minister Antonio Guterres said in an opening address to more than 50 OSCE leaders.

Russia has pushed for changes to the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty ever since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991, and Western nations hope changes will address Moscow's concerns over the military balance in Europe.

"This work must be aimed at limiting the military potential of alliances, not building up the military potential on foreign territories, limiting more broadly than now the circle of categories of military equipment," Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told the summit.
U.S. Vice President Al Gore described the decision as "an important step" to increase European security.

"The work that lies ahead to adapt the CFE treaty is crucial, crucial to maintain stability and crucial to build confidence in today's undivided Europe," British Prime Minister John Major told the OSCE, grouping the United States and Canada with all European nations.
French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl added their voices in support of an adapted CFE treaty, saying it would help anchor security on the continent.
A senior U.S. official said it was clear that the CFE treaty had to be changed because arms limits had been based on two military alliances, NATO and the now-defunct Warsaw Pact.

Without specifically mentioning Russia, he cautioned that no nation should try to negotiate for higher arms quotas on the pretext that NATO was planning to expand eastwards to take in former Soviet satellites, such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. Moscow fiercely opposes any such expansion.
"We are not going into the negotiations with the idea that any country should be compensated for NATO enlargement," the U.S. official told reporters.
"We have to replace the bloc-to-bloc limits and I think that national ceilings is the way this will be done," he added.
Thirty countries are now signatories to the treaty, negotiated under the auspices of the OSCE. The new talks will take place in January in Vienna where the organisation is based.
A West European official said more European nations could join in the new talks and there was scope for new categories of military hardware to be added to the limits quotas, such as naval equipment.

Signatory states destroyed more than 50,000 pieces of military equipment within a November 17, 1995 deadline set down in the treaty. The total included nearly 19,000 battle tanks, 18,000 armoured vehicles and thousands of pieces of artillery, combat aircraft and attack helicopters.

But before the 1995 date, Moscow announced it could not meet its obligations because it said that reducing military might on its frontiers would ruin its defence capabilities. It cited particular concern over its southern flank near the troubled Caucasus, where Russian troops were fighting Chechen rebels.

The United States accepted Moscow's argument and put pressure on its NATO allies to agree to update the CFE pact, despite concern from Norway and Turkey over any increase in Russian military weapons near their borders.
